Below is an evidence-backed overview of major benchmarks used to evaluate automated program repair (APR), organized by their scope, construction, and evaluation protocols. Where possible, we summarize sizes, bug types, and how fixes are validated, and highlight known limitations and emerging trends.

# Landscape and Taxonomy

Program repair benchmarks span three broad categories: (1) repository-scale, issue/PR–driven defects (e.g., SWE-bench and derivatives), (2) unit-test–driven bugs in real-world or classic problems (e.g., Defects4J, QuixBugs, JSBench-inspired corpora), and (3) large execution-based corpora from programming problems (e.g., FixEval) designed for ML training and evaluation. <cite id="f8ab0254-0">DeepFix and Refactory are student assignment–based; QuixBugs and Defects4J provide real-world programs with test suites; FIXEVAL is substantially larger (54M Java, 61M Python LOC) and spans multi-line to multi-file bugs</cite> <cite id="f8ab0254-1">Recent APR papers typically evaluate on Defects4J (Java) and QuixBugs (Java/Python), often stratified into Single-Function/Single-Hunk/Single-Line scenarios, and sometimes add HumanEval-Java for generalizability with leakage control</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-4">Defects4J provides pairs of buggy/fixed versions and developer test suites; evaluations often split into Defects4J 1.2 (391 bugs) and 2.0 (438 bugs), with single-hunk and single-line subsets</cite> <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite collects 300 real software problems across popular repos with problem descriptions, reproduction steps, and automated test harnesses, reported with Pass@1</cite>.

# Core Benchmarks and What They Contain

Defects4J (Java, unit-test–driven)
- Construction and size: <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">Defects4J contains 434 real bugs across six Java projects (e.g., JFreeChart, Closure Compiler, Apache Commons, Mockito, Joda-Time), with a buggy and fixed version per bug and developer test suites; after reproducibility and environment constraints, many studies use 391 bugs (v1.2) and 438 bugs (v2.0), and exclude projects with non-JUnit testing or unstable artifacts</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-0">Some analyses remove Closure Compiler due to nonstandard JUnit tests, using 224 program versions across four projects</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-2">Excluded projects may have flaky artifacts or non-reproducible setups; e.g., Closure Compiler dropped for custom tests and Mockito for instability</cite>.
- Use: <cite id="3bd6acb8-4">Pairs of buggy/patched versions and unit tests enable repair proposals validated by test passes; evaluations commonly stratify by bug granularity and report resolve rates</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">The dataset also supports fault localization and test-case engineering tasks</cite>.

QuixBugs (Classic algorithmic bugs, Java/Python)
- Construction and size: <cite id="f8ab0254-0">QuixBugs consists of 40 function-level “classic” bugs, originally in Python and later translated to Java, each with multiple test inputs and expected outputs</cite> <cite id="f8ab0254-1">QuixBugs-Java and QuixBugs-Python are often treated together; in Java, all single-hunk bugs correspond to single-line fixes, while the Python version contains only single-line fixes</cite>.
- Use: <cite id="f8ab0254-2">Simple, isolated bugs make QuixBugs suitable for probing basic transformation and debugging heuristics; recent models achieve 95% fix rates on the 40-bug Java set</cite>.

ManyBugs and IntroClass (C/educational Java)
- Construction and size: <cite id="f8ab0254-3">ManyBugs collects 185 C bugs from nine open-source projects with developer-written tests, but only 91 were reproducible in a later study</cite> <cite id="f8ab0254-4">IntroClassJava (Refactory) and Bugs.jar have been used historically; early tools were often evaluated on proprietary datasets before being ported to Defects4J</cite>.
- Use: <cite id="f8ab0254-4">These earlier benchmarks enabled early APR tool evaluations and learning baselines (e.g., GenProg, Nopol), but adoption has concentrated on Defects4J and QuixBugs over time</cite> <cite id="f8ab0254-4">The empirical review reports 38 evaluations across 24 tools, with Defects4J and QuixBugs dominating</cite>.

JavaScript and Python benchmarks (JSBench/JS-inspired, Python corpora)
- Construction: <cite id="6cd98ffe-2">A widely used JavaScript repair evaluation corpus was derived from BugsJS, containing reproducible JavaScript bugs from 10 GitHub projects, yielding 18,736 files with both single- and multi-line bugs</cite>. <cite id="6cd98ffe-1">Python benchmarks like EXCEPY aggregate 180 faults across 15 open-source projects to evaluate detection and repair, emphasizing real-world reproducibility and tool comparisons</cite>.
- Use: <cite id="6cd98ffe-2">These datasets aim to be representative of real-world complexity and support both white-box and black-box evaluations</cite>.

SWE-bench and SWE-bench Lite (Repository-scale, issue/PR defects)
- Construction and scope: <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite includes 300 real software problems drawn from popular GitHub repositories across multiple languages and frameworks (e.g., Django, Flask, NumPy, Pandas), each with problem descriptions, reproduction steps, expected outcomes, and an automated testing framework for verification</cite>.
- Use and metrics: <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">Evaluations typically report Pass@1 on the full set and across languages; problems reflect end-to-end bug fixing in genuine codebases, testing integration and change-management realism</cite>.

FixEval (Execution-based, programming problems)
- Construction and scale: <cite id="f8ab0254-0">FIXEVAL aggregates 712K Java and 3.28M Python submissions with injected bugs, yielding 54M LOC (Java) and 61M LOC (Python), with bugs spanning one line to multi-file; unlike student assignment datasets, it emphasizes diverse sizes and difficulties while enabling ML model training</cite>.
- Use: <cite id="f8ab0254-0">Design targets execution-based evaluation of fixes at scale, contrasting with Defects4J’s real-world patches and QuixBugs’s classic, single-line defects</cite>.

# Evaluation Protocols, Metrics, and Pitfalls

Metrics and protocols
- Resolve rate and pass@1: <cite id="f8ab0254-2">For repository-level benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and Defects4J v2.0, results are typically reported as resolve rate (e.g., percentage of bugs fully resolved), while for function-level benchmarks (QuixBugs, HumanEval-Java), percentage of correctly fixed bugs under strict evaluation is used</cite>. <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite commonly uses Pass@1 as the primary metric</cite>.
- Granularity filtering: <cite id="f8ab0254-1">Benchmarks are often stratified into Single-Function, Single-Hunk, and Single-Line categories; single-line is nested within single-hunk and function-level, reflecting varying repair complexity</cite>. <cite id="f8ab0254-3">Recent studies filter to single-function/hunk/line settings within larger datasets to focus on local repairs</cite>.

Data quality and bias pitfalls
- Flaky and “future” tests: <cite id="3bd6acb8-1">Defects4J evaluations can be biased by “future tests” that change during bug resolution; prior work shows fault-triggering tests evolve from bug creation to fix, and modified tests can mislead fault localization and repair evaluation</cite>. <cite id="3bd6acb8-1">Analyses document that some tests may not accurately reflect intended behavior and that such issues affect generalizability across APR tasks</cite>.
- Benchmark representativeness and underuse: <cite id="f8ab0254-4">Despite dominance, Defects4J and QuixBugs are not the only options; several tools were evaluated on proprietary datasets before being ported, and some benchmarks (e.g., Bugs.jar, IntroClass) are rarely used today</cite>. <cite id="f8ab0254-4">The review observes a gap between the number of repair tools and the number of benchmarks used, with Defects4J and QuixBugs accounting for most evaluations</cite>.
- Leakage control: <cite id="f8ab0254-1">HumanEval-Java injects bugs into known, tested programs and releases the Java conversion after GPT-3.5 training to reduce data leakage risk and improve generalizability checks</cite>.

# Notable Suites by Domain and Trend Lines

Java (real-world and repository-scale)
- Defects4J remains the canonical suite for Java APR, with multiple versions and strong tool coverage, though project-specific issues (e.g., Closure Compiler) and test evolution biases demand caution. <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">Defects4J pairs buggy/fixed versions and unit tests and supports broader SE research tasks</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-0">Excluding non-JUnit projects improves comparability</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-1">Test evolution and “future tests” can bias evaluation</cite>.
- QuixBugs provides isolated, classic bugs to probe core transformation and debugging capabilities. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">Java and Python versions enable cross-language comparison; single-line fixes facilitate strong baselines for syntactic/one-liner repairs</cite>.
- Emerging repo-level benchmarks: <cite id="f8ab0254-2">Work on SWE-bench Verified reports resolve rates for 500 instances</cite> and <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite offers 300 authentic problems with automated test harnesses and Pass@1</cite>.

JavaScript and Python
- JSBench lineage and BugsJS-derived corpora emphasize real-world bugs and multi-line edits: <cite id="6cd98ffe-2">A BugsJS-derived dataset with 10 repos and 18,736 files captures single- and multi-line bugs for end-to-end repair and ML training</cite>. <cite id="6cd98ffe-1">Python EXCEPY aggregates 180 faults across 15 projects to benchmark detection and repair pipelines</cite>.

C/C++ and educational settings
- ManyBugs and IntroClass remain historical baselines: <cite id="f8ab0254-3">ManyBugs’ 185 C bugs (91 reproducible) and IntroClass/Refactory for introductory Java have informed early learning-based and search-based approaches</cite>. <cite id="f8ab0254-4">GenProg, Prophet, and Angelix achieved 27/105, 42/105, and 28/105 fixes on ManyBugs with a subset equivalent to human patches</cite> <cite id="6cd98ffe-4">SemFix and other semantic-based tools also show strong results on Java; learning-based methods have gained attention and performance</cite>.

Machine-learning code (Python/TF)
- DeepFix and TensorFix target ML codebases; DeepFix is assignment-based with unit tests, while TensorFix focuses on TensorFlow graphs and dataflows. <cite id="f8ab0254-0">DeepFix originates from student assignments with unit tests, contrasting with real-world repo datasets like Defects4J</cite>. <cite id="f8ab0254-3">Surveys note an emphasis on single-function bugs across languages and include TensorFlow-focused datasets as part of the broader landscape</cite>.

# How to Choose and Use Benchmarks

- Match difficulty and scope to your method:
  - Classic/algorithmic bugs (QuixBugs) stress syntactic/one-liner repairs and quick progress on heuristics and transformations. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">QuixBugs-Java/Python provide 40 small, well-scoped bugs with clear single-line/single-hunk categories</cite>.
  - Real-world unit-test–driven Java (Defects4J) measures end-to-end effectiveness on larger codebases with evolving patches/tests. <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">Pairs of buggy/fixed versions and JUnit suites enable patch synthesis and validation</cite>, but <cite id="3bd6acb8-1">test evolution and “future tests” can bias evaluation</cite>.
  - Repository-scale issues (SWE-bench/SWE-bench Lite) assess integration, cross-file edits, and CI/test flakiness. <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">Problems are drawn from genuine projects (Django, Flask, NumPy, Pandas) with automated verification and Pass@1</cite>.
  - Large execution-based corpora (FixEval) enable ML training and stress diverse bug sizes and failure modes. <cite id="f8ab0254-0">54M LOC (Java) and 61M LOC (Python) with 712K Java/3.28M Python submissions produce multi-line to multi-file bugs and support execution-based evaluation</cite>.

- Report protocols that matter:
  - State the metric (resolve rate, Pass@1, strict vs relaxed), the subset (single-line/hunk/function), and whether repairs are pass@1 or allow multi-attempt. <cite id="f8ab0254-2">Defects4J and SWE-bench use resolve rate and Pass@1 across subsets; strict evaluation checks exact fix correctness</cite>.
  - Control for leakage and environment drift; prefer post-training injections (e.g., HumanEval-Java) and rebase to current toolchains. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">HumanEval-Java converts and injects bugs post-GPT-3.5 training to mitigate leakage</cite>.
  - Audit test stability and timeline; identify and exclude “future tests” or perform sensitivity analyses. <cite id="3bd6acb8-1">Comprehensive analysis of test evolution in Defects4J shows fault-triggering tests change over time, affecting evaluation</cite>.
  - Prefer broader coverage across languages and projects to avoid narrow bias; include cross-language variants when possible. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">QuixBugs exists in Java and Python with aligned bug sets</cite> <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite spans multiple languages and frameworks</cite>.

# Representative Results and What They Imply

- Granularity matters. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">Single-line bugs are a subset of single-hunk, which is a subset of single-function; category choice affects comparability</cite>. <cite id="f8ab0254-2">On QuixBugs (40 Java), execution-grounded reinforcement learning achieved 95% (38/40), while base models already scored 90%, indicating substantial headroom on simple tasks</cite>.
- Real-world Java remains challenging. <cite id="f8ab0254-3">Defects4J v1.2 and v2.0 aggregate hundreds of bugs with developer tests; the best Java tools can correctly fix more than 50% of bugs on Defects4J</cite>, and <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">pairwise bug/patch availability and JUnit harnesses enable direct repair-to-test validation</cite>.
- Repository-scale benchmarks expose different skills. <cite id="f8ab0254-2">On SWE-bench Verified (500 instances), a reinforcement-learning–based model reached 84.5% function-level repair, suggesting transfer from repository-level training to isolated function repairs</cite> and <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite reports Pass@1 across 300 authentic problems with automated test frameworks</cite>.
- Scale and diversity improve realism. <cite id="f8ab0254-0">FIXEVAL’s 54M/61M LOC and multi-million submission base targets heterogeneous bug sizes and behaviors, enabling training and evaluation under execution-based criteria</cite>.
- Historical baselines matter for trend context. <cite id="f8ab0254-4">Early tool evaluations on ManyBugs/IntroClass and proprietary datasets paved the way for Defects4J/QuixBugs dominance</cite>, and <cite id="6cd98ffe-4">learning-based tools have increasingly outperformed search/semantic baselines on Java</cite>.

# Practical Checklist for Benchmark Use

- Define the unit of evaluation (bug/issue), the allowed edit scope (function/hunk/file), and the test harness (unit tests vs. end-to-end CI). <cite id="f8ab0254-2">Defects4J uses resolve rate; QuixBugs uses correctness under strict evaluation; SWE-bench uses Pass@1</cite>.
- Validate test stability across the bug lifecycle and report sensitivity to flaky/future tests. <cite id="3bd6acb8-1">Test evolution and irrelevance are documented risks in Defects4J</cite>.
- Control for data leakage; prefer post-training bug injection or non-overlapping splits. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">HumanEval-Java injects bugs after GPT-3.5 training</cite>.
- Report per-language and per-category breakdowns to enable fair cross-benchmark comparisons. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">QuixBugs-Java and -Python align on classic bugs; category-wise breakdowns clarify capabilities</cite> <cite id="f8ab0254-3">Defects4J/QuixBugs/ManyBugs category stats help interpret generalization</cite>.
- Use multiple suites to triangulate claims: classic (QuixBugs) for fundamentals, Java real-world (Defects4J) for unit-test robustness, repository-scale (SWE-bench) for end-to-end integration, and large execution corpora (FixEval) for scale and diversity. <cite id="f8ab0254-0">FIXEVAL enables large-scale ML training and evaluation</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">Defects4J offers unit-test validation</cite> <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite offers authentic, automated verification</cite>.

# Summary

The APR benchmark ecosystem has matured from small, classic problem sets to large, diverse, and realistic suites spanning unit-test–driven Java (Defects4J), isolated classic bugs (QuixBugs), repository-scale software engineering (SWE-bench/SWE-bench Lite), and massive execution-based corpora (FixEval). <cite id="f8ab0254-0">FIXEVAL’s scale and diverse bug sizes address earlier limitations of student assignment datasets</cite>, while <cite id="3bd6acb8-1">Defects4J’s test evolution issues</cite> and <cite id="f8ab0254-1">leakage controls</cite> highlight best practices for fair evaluation. <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench and SWE-bench Lite push end-to-end, integration-aware repair</cite>, and <cite id="f8ab0254-2">recent model advances show strong performance on classic and Java benchmarks</cite>, setting the stage for broader deployment and continued benchmark evolution at repository scale. <cite id="f8ab0254-4">Across languages, Defects4J and QuixBugs dominate current evaluations, though emerging suites broaden coverage and realism</cite>.

Where possible, we summarize sizes, bug types, and how fixes are validated, and highlight known limitations and emerging trends.

# Landscape and Taxonomy

Program repair benchmarks span three broad categories: (1) repository-scale, issue/PR–driven defects (e.g., SWE-bench and derivatives), (2) unit-test–driven bugs in real-world or classic problems (e.g., Defects4J, QuixBugs, JSBench-inspired corpora), and (3) large execution-based corpora from programming problems (e.g., FixEval) designed for ML training and evaluation. <cite id="f8ab0254-0">DeepFix and Refactory are student assignment–based; QuixBugs and Defects4J provide real-world programs with test suites; FIXEVAL is substantially larger (54M Java, 61M Python LOC) and spans multi-line to multi-file bugs</cite> <cite id="f8ab0254-1">Recent APR papers typically evaluate on Defects4J (Java) and QuixBugs (Java/Python), often stratified into Single-Function/Single-Hunk/Single-Line scenarios, and sometimes add HumanEval-Java for generalizability with leakage control</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-4">Defects4J provides pairs of buggy/fixed versions and developer test suites; evaluations often split into Defects4J 1.2 (391 bugs) and 2.0 (438 bugs), with single-hunk and single-line subsets</cite> <cite id="6cd98ffe-3">SWE-bench Lite collects 300 real software problems across popular repos with problem descriptions, reproduction steps, and automated test harnesses, reported with Pass@1</cite>.

# Core Benchmarks and What They Contain

- Construction and size: <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">Defects4J contains 434 real bugs across six Java projects (e.g., JFreeChart, Closure Compiler, Apache Commons, Mockito, Joda-Time), with a buggy and fixed version per bug and developer test suites; after reproducibility and environment constraints, many studies use 391 bugs (v1.2) and 438 bugs (v2.0), and exclude projects with non-JUnit testing or unstable artifacts</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-0">Some analyses remove Closure Compiler due to nonstandard JUnit tests, using 224 program versions across four projects</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-2">Excluded projects may have flaky artifacts or non-reproducible setups; e.g., Closure Compiler dropped for custom tests and Mockito for instability</cite>.
- Use: <cite id="3bd6acb8-4">Pairs of buggy/patched versions and unit tests enable repair proposals validated by test passes; evaluations commonly stratify by bug granularity and report resolve rates</cite> <cite id="3bd6acb8-3">The dataset also supports fault localization and test-case engineering tasks</cite>.

QuixBugs (Classic algorithmic bugs, Java/Python)
- Construction and size: <cite id="f8ab0254-0">QuixBugs consists of 40 function-level “classic” bugs, originally in Python and later translated to Java, each with multiple test inputs and expected outputs</cite> <cite id="f8ab0254-1">QuixBugs-Java and QuixBugs-Python are often treated together; in Java, all single-hunk bugs correspond to single-line fixes, while the Python version contains only single-line fixes</cite>.

Metrics and protocols

# How to Choose and Use Benchmarks

- Match difficulty and scope to your method:
  - Classic/algorithmic bugs (QuixBugs) stress syntactic/one-liner repairs and quick progress on heuristics and transformations. <cite id="f8ab0254-1">QuixBugs-Java/Python provide 40 small, well-scoped bugs with clear single-line/single-hunk categories</cite>.

Below we synthesize categories of real-world program defects that are systematically underrepresented or absent from standard program repair benchmarks, and explain why. We ground each category in evidence from widely used APR datasets and studies that analyze their coverage and limitations.

Summary of the coverage gap
Across the most widely used APR benchmarks—Defects4J (Java), QuixBugs (Java/Python), Bugs.jar, IntroClassJava, and newer collections like RepoBugs/SBPjit/Trove—there is a consistent emphasis on small, code-level bugs that can be isolated, reproduced with tests, and fixed within a single function or hunk, while large classes of real-world defects are excluded by design or lack of representation. <cite id="ca551466-0">Defects4J dominates in repairability and tools overfit it; the authors explicitly hypothesize that differences in the distribution of bug types across benchmarks drive these patterns</cite>. <cite id="ca551466-3">QuixBugs consists entirely of one-line bugs in classic programming problems, with single-function/single-hunk scope in both Java and Python</cite>, and <cite id="ca551466-4">DeepFix and Refactory are courseware/student-submission datasets with unit tests, while Defects4J provides real-world programs but at a narrower scope than newer, much larger execution-based corpora</cite>.

1) Build, configuration, and meta-level defects
- Exclusion by benchmark criteria: Defects4J explicitly excludes bugs in build systems, configuration files, documentation, and tests, focusing instead on source-code-level faults reproducible via test changes. <cite id="b13289a1-3">Each real bug in Defects4J must be related to source code, reproducible with tests, and isolated from unrelated changes; fixes in build/config/documentation/tests are not included</cite>. This means defects that manifest through wrong environment variables, misconfigured CI, dependency conflicts, or patching Makefiles/Maven/Gradle scripts are absent from evaluation.
- Consequence: repair systems are not exercised on meta-level causes of failures that are pervasive in production (e.g., Cargo Cult code in configs, POM/XML/JSON schema errors, environment-specific secrets/mixups), even though such fixes can be crucial to deployability.

2) Concurrency and data-race bugs
- Interprocedural/multi-threaded complexity is scarce: <cite id="e04f8178-1">Most defects in Defects4J span multiple methods, classes, or packages and rely on complex contexts, configuration, databases, or external state, so researchers often filter to subsets where a single focal method suffices</cite>. <cite id="ca551466-3">QuixBugs programs are small and classic-problem oriented, with single-line/single-hunk fixes and no cross-method interactions</cite>. These properties make data races, lock-order deadlocks, thread-scope races, and other concurrency defects rare in these datasets, which assume thread-local or deterministic execution for repair modeling.
- Test isolation limits concurrency coverage: <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J requires bugs to be reproducible with a test that passes on the fixed version but fails on the buggy version</cite>. In practice, reproducing race conditions reliably requires non-deterministic or timing-sensitive setups, which many benchmarked tools and studies do not support.

3) Memory safety and undefined behavior (UB) defects
- Dataset scope and failure types: While QuixBugs enumerates concrete failure types, it emphasizes incorrect output, stack overflow, index-out-of-bounds, infinite loops, null pointer, and “current modification” failures for small academic programs. <cite id="e04f8178-4">QuixBugs programs have 6 distinct failure types: incorrect output (26), stack overflow (5), index out of bounds (5), infinite loop (3), null pointer (2), and current modification (2)</cite>. This distribution understates memory-model and pointer-related defects common in production (e.g., dangling pointers, use-after-free, double-free, buffer overflows) and the interplay with unsafe casts or C/C++ idioms absent from Java-focused repair suites.
- Tooling bias and null-related prevalence: <cite id="b13289a1-2">Defects4J-derived evaluations often focus on null pointer dereferences, array index out-of-bounds, and number format exceptions</cite>, and <cite id="b13289a1-4">authors note Defects4J contains a considerable number of null pointer bugs, favoring approaches that detect and fix null-related issues with templates</cite>. This reflects an overemphasis on null and numeric index faults rather than broader memory-safety/UB categories.

4) I/O, protocol, and environment-specific defects
- Many real-world bugs stem from file system interactions, network protocol mismatches, locale/encoding, and environment-sensitive behavior (race with GC, signal handling, time zones). <cite id="e04f8178-1">Defects4J defects are filtered to remove reliance on “complex contexts, configuration files, databases, or external states” to serve as side-effect-free units</cite>, and <cite id="ca551466-0">the distribution of bug types differs across benchmarks, with Defects4J being dominant</cite>. These design choices systematically remove I/O/protocol/environment triggers that are essential to many defects in production.
- Practical consequence: APR tools trained/evaluated on these datasets rarely confront file-descriptor leaks, deserialization exploits, TLS/HTTP misordering, or OS-level interop issues, even though such bugs are common in deployed systems.

5) Security vulnerabilities and cross-process/web-of-trust issues
- While some security flaws (e.g., SQLi, XSS) may appear in mined Java corpora, repair benchmarks emphasize code-local, reproducible vulnerabilities with deterministic tests. <cite id="ca551466-3">QuixBugs exposes bugs via failing JUnit tests and focuses on single-line fixes</cite>, and <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J bugs are isolated and not about test code itself</cite>. Cross-site/scripting, deserialization gadget chains, insecure deserialization, weak cryptography, and trust management often require broader application state, external services, or human interaction—conditions that are absent or underrepresented in standard suites.
- Benchmark curation realities: <cite id="ca551466-0">Researchers frequently filter out complex, multi-file, or configuration-dependent defects from Defects4J, and tool overfitting is observed when evaluated on other datasets</cite>, reinforcing that cross-component security patterns are likely under-sampled.

6) Multi-file, interprocedural, and ecosystem-scale defects
- Real-world regressions often span multiple files, call graphs, and even repositories (e.g., macro/mixin misuse, template parameter errors, dependency API breakage). <cite id="e04f8178-1">A large fraction of Defects4J defects span multiple methods/classes/packages and rely on complex contexts, leading to curated subsets that strip these dependencies</cite>. <cite id="ca551466-3">QuixBugs programs are logically simple and independent</cite>, and <cite id="ca551466-4">student-submission datasets like DeepFix/Refactory are small and unit-test driven</cite>. These constraints exclude defects that require cross-file refactoring, macro expansion, or ecosystem-level changes.
- Scope bias toward Java ecosystems: <cite id="ca551466-3">Evaluation centers on Java projects in Defects4J and QuixBugs (Java/Python)</cite>, leaving polyglot production stacks (e.g., Python/Node/Go integrations) and language-specific idioms underrepresented.

7) Non-deterministic and heisenbugs (timing, race, latent state)
- Repair evaluation often demands deterministic triggers, which filters out timing-sensitive heisenbugs. <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J requires reproducibility with tests that fail on the buggy version and pass on the fixed one</cite>, and <cite id="e04f8178-1">pragmatic filtering to “focal method” units removes defects triggered by interprocedural contexts, databases, or external state</cite>. In practice, many production defects manifest only under load, specific OS versions, or with certain drivers, and require flakiness-aware detection and patching—capabilities seldom exercised on standard benchmarks.
- QuixBugs’ unit-level, single-line focus further limits exposure to flakiness and complex timing interactions.

8) Distributional bias toward specific defect classes and repair scenarios
- Single-line/one-hunk dominance: <cite id="ca551466-3">All QuixBugs-Python bugs are single-line/single-hunk/single-function, and QuixBugs-Java is overwhelmingly single-line/single-hunk</cite>, while <cite id="ca551466-1">Defects4J is partitioned into single-function/single-hunk/single-line scenarios with corresponding statistics</cite>. This skews APR towards templateable fixes and away from multi-statement refactorings, complex logic restructuring, or design-pattern changes.
- Concentration of null and numeric defects: <cite id="b13289a1-4">Defects4J’s large null-pointer presence favors approaches with explicit null detection and fix templates, making the dataset reflect a biased distribution rather than the natural world</cite>, and <cite id="b13289a1-2">Defects4J-derived evaluations often enumerate null pointer, array index out-of-bound, and number format exceptions</cite>. These categories are overrepresented relative to, say, concurrency, protocol, or configuration-origin bugs.

Structural reasons behind the gap
- Selection and isolation criteria: <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J’s inclusion requires source-code-related, reproducible-by-tests, and fix-isolated bugs; build/config/doc/test fixes are excluded</cite>. <cite id="ca551466-0">Benchmark differences in bug-type distributions and tool overfitting to Defects4J are empirically observed</cite>. <cite id="e04f8178-1">Curators often filter out complex interprocedural contexts and external dependencies to enable unit-test-based repair</cite>.
- Scope and scale: <cite id="ca551466-3">QuixBugs is small-scale and one-line, with JUnit-failures-only exposure</cite> and <cite id="ca551466-4">student assignment/problem-based datasets emphasize unit tests and single-function edits</cite>, whereas real-world programs exhibit cross-function, cross-project, and polyglot complexity.
- Failure-mode coverage: <cite id="e04f8178-4">QuixBugs exposes failure types like incorrect output, stack overflow, index out of bounds, infinite loops, null pointer, and current modification</cite>, which, while concrete, omit broader categories like memory corruption, race-induced nondeterminism, and environment-triggered crashes.

Emerging steps toward broader coverage
- Broader and more execution-heavy corpora: <cite id="ca551466-4">FIXEVAL is substantially larger than Defects4J and QuixBugs, spans multi-line bugs from 712K Java and 3.28M Python submissions, and is designed for execution-based evaluation, enabling training of ML models</cite>. The authors argue such scale and diversity make it more representative than unit-test-only datasets.
- Single-line contest bug collections: <cite id="ca551466-3">ConDefect aggregates single-line contest bugs in Java and Python from 645 tasks published after a training cutoff, reducing data leakage risk</cite>, yet it still emphasizes line-level edits and contest contexts, not broader defect classes.
- Concurrency-focused efforts: <cite id="e04f8178-1">Researchers note the need to handle interprocedural context and cross-method interactions, and propose filtering and modeling strategies to include such defects</cite>, indicating nascent steps to incorporate multi-method and external-state triggers.

Practical implications and guidance for researchers
- Categories to prioritize adding: build/config/dependency/environment bugs; cross-threading and data races; memory safety/UB (dangling pointers, buffer overflows); I/O/protocol and locale/encoding issues; cross-process/web-of-trust security flaws; and polyglot, multi-file defects that require refactorings and ecosystem changes. <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J’s explicit exclusion of build/config/test fixes</cite> and <cite id="e04f8178-1">removal of external state and complex contexts</cite> identify concrete gaps to address.

1) Build, configuration, and meta-level defects
- Exclusion by benchmark criteria: Defects4J explicitly excludes bugs in build systems, configuration files, documentation, and tests, focusing instead on source-code-level faults reproducible via test changes. <cite id="b13289a1-3">Each real bug in Defects4J must be related to source code, reproducible with tests, and isolated from unrelated changes; fixes in build/config/documentation/tests are not included</cite>. - Consequence: repair systems are not exercised on meta-level causes of failures that are pervasive in production (e.g., Cargo Cult code in configs, POM/XML/JSON schema errors, environment-specific secrets/mixups), even though such fixes can be crucial to deployability.

2) Concurrency and data-race bugs
- Interprocedural/multi-threaded complexity is scarce: <cite id="e04f8178-1">Most defects in Defects4J span multiple methods, classes, or packages and rely on complex contexts, configuration, databases, or external state, so researchers often filter to subsets where a single focal method suffices</cite>. <cite id="ca551466-3">QuixBugs programs are small and classic-problem oriented, with single-line/single-hunk fixes and no cross-method interactions</cite>. These properties make data races, lock-order deadlocks, thread-scope races, and other concurrency defects rare in these datasets, which assume thread-local or deterministic execution for repair modeling.
- Test isolation limits concurrency coverage: <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J requires bugs to be reproducible with a test that passes on the fixed version but fails on the buggy version</cite>. In practice, reproducing race conditions reliably requires non-deterministic or timing-sensitive setups, which many benchmarked tools and studies do not support.

3) Memory safety and undefined behavior (UB) defects
- Dataset scope and failure types: While QuixBugs enumerates concrete failure types, it emphasizes incorrect output, stack overflow, index-out-of-bounds, infinite loops, null pointer, and “current modification” failures for small academic programs. <cite id="e04f8178-4">QuixBugs programs have 6 distinct failure types: incorrect output (26), stack overflow (5), index out of bounds (5), infinite loop (3), null pointer (2), and current modification (2)</cite>. These design choices systematically remove I/O/protocol/environment triggers that are essential to many defects in production.
- Practical consequence: APR tools trained/evaluated on these datasets rarely confront file-descriptor leaks, deserialization exploits, TLS/HTTP misordering, or OS-level interop issues, even though such bugs are common in deployed systems.

5) Security vulnerabilities and cross-process/web-of-trust issues

- Repair evaluation often demands deterministic triggers, which filters out timing-sensitive heisenbugs. <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J requires reproducibility with tests that fail on the buggy version and pass on the fixed one</cite>, and <cite id="e04f8178-1">pragmatic filtering to “focal method” units removes defects triggered by interprocedural contexts, databases, or external state</cite>. - Single-line/one-hunk dominance: <cite id="ca551466-3">All QuixBugs-Python bugs are single-line/single-hunk/single-function, and QuixBugs-Java is overwhelmingly single-line/single-hunk</cite>, while <cite id="ca551466-1">Defects4J is partitioned into single-function/single-hunk/single-line scenarios with corresponding statistics</cite>. This skews APR towards templateable fixes and away from multi-statement refactorings, complex logic restructuring, or design-pattern changes.

These categories are overrepresented relative to, say, concurrency, protocol, or configuration-origin bugs.

Structural reasons behind the gap
- Selection and isolation criteria: <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J’s inclusion requires source-code-related, reproducible-by-tests, and fix-isolated bugs; build/config/doc/test fixes are excluded</cite>. <cite id="ca551466-0">Benchmark differences in bug-type distributions and tool overfitting to Defects4J are empirically observed</cite>. <cite id="e04f8178-1">Curators often filter out complex interprocedural contexts and external dependencies to enable unit-test-based repair</cite>.

- Broader and more execution-heavy corpora: <cite id="ca551466-4">FIXEVAL is substantially larger than Defects4J and QuixBugs, spans multi-line bugs from 712K Java and 3.28M Python submissions, and is designed for execution-based evaluation, enabling training of ML models</cite>. Practical implications and guidance for researchers
- Categories to prioritize adding: build/config/dependency/environment bugs; cross-threading and data races; memory safety/UB (dangling pointers, buffer overflows); I/O/protocol and locale/encoding issues; cross-process/web-of-trust security flaws; and polyglot, multi-file defects that require refactorings and ecosystem changes. <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J’s explicit exclusion of build/config/test fixes</cite> and <cite id="e04f8178-1">removal of external state and complex contexts</cite> identify concrete gaps to address.
- Evaluate under non-determinism: include flakiness-aware test harnesses and timing/race triggers to expose heisenbugs. <cite id="b13289a1-3">Defects4J’s test-based reproducibility requirement</cite> and <cite id="e04f8178-1">focal-method filtering</cite> highlight where current tools are not stressed.
- Diversify failure types: augment datasets with memory-model violations, protocol anomalies, and environment-sensitive regressions, and report category-stratified repair metrics to avoid biasing toward null/IOOBounds/number-format classes. <cite id="e04f8178-4">QuixBugs’ failure-type distribution</cite> and <cite id="b13289a1-4">Defects4J’s null-dominance</cite> provide baselines to correct.

Title: Infrared: A Meta Bug Detector
Snippet: In this experiment, we evaluate the effectiveness of Infrared in catching bugs from real-world codebases. This is the typical way static bug finders are used except in our case bugs are already identified. For groundtruth, we extract 79 bugs from Defects4J [Just et al. 2014], arguably the most well-established dataset of bugs in Java programs. Title: Attention Please: Consider Mockito when Evaluating Newly Released Automated Program Repair Techniques

Four tools (i.e., ACS, SOFix, CapGen, and Elixir) do not select Closure and three of them (except for Elixir) clearly explain the reason is that this project uses a customized testing format instead of JUnit test. Title: ARJA: Automated Repair of Java Programs via Multi-Objective Genetic Programming
Snippet: In summary, through careful manual assessment, we find that ARJA can synthesize a correct patch for at least 18 bugs in Defects4J. To the best of our knowledge, some of the 18 bugs have never been fixed correctly by existing repair systems in the literature. Furthermore, ARJA is able to generate correct patches for several multi-location bugs, which is impossible for most of the other repair approaches. 

Note that we do not focus on the number of correctly repaired bugs on the Defects4J dataset when comparing ARJA with other approaches that are not based on the redundancy assumption (e.g., Nopol). Nowadays, it is common knowledge that different kinds of repair techniques can be better at addressing different classes of bugs. For example, although Nopol that targets conditional statement bugs can only fix 5 bugs correctly on the same dataset [7], 3 of them cannot be repaired correctly by ARJA. So the number of correct fixes by different categories of repair techniques would strongly depend on how the dataset tested was built [14]. Also, we cannot expect that the 224 bugs in Defects4J can truly reflect the natural distribution of real-world bugs. For instance, Defects4J indeed contains a considerable number of null pointer bugs, so it may favor those approaches that can explicitly conduct null pointer detection with fix templates (e.g., PAR [54] and ACS [46]). Compared to such approaches, ARJA is a more generic repair approach. 

In contrast, ARJA and jGenProg can be compared meaningfully on the Defects4J dataset in terms of the number of bugs fixed or correctly fixed, because both of them typically belong to redundancy-based repair techniques and use GP to explore the search space. ARJA performs much better than jGenProg, which clearly validates the improvement of GP search in ARJA. 

To facilitate re-examination by the other researchers, we provide a detailed explanation of the correctness for each correct patch generated by ARJA, publicly available at GitHub. 21

In summary, through careful manual assessment, we find that ARJA can synthesize a correct patch for at least 18 bugs in Defects4J. To the best of our knowledge, some of the 18 bugs have never been fixed correctly by existing repair systems in the literature.
